notes.text:
consider this and addd in our engine --Here is why Vidyut correctly applies it:
1. Rule 8.4.68 targets the phoneme 'अ' anywhere, not just at the end of a word.
If we break down रामम् phonetically, it is:
र् + आ + म् + अ + म्
Even though the word itself terminates in a halant consonant ('म्'), there is a short 'अ' sitting right in the middle of that final syllable. Rule 8.4.68 applies to every short 'अ' that exists in the final string, regardless of what letter the word ends with.
2. The "Vivṛta" vs. "Saṃvṛta" mechanism
Throughout the entire Aṣṭādhyāyī, Pāṇini relies on a clever computational fiction: he artificially treats the short 'अ' as vivṛta (fully open). He does this so that short 'अ' and long 'आ' share the exact same mouth effort, making them savarṇa (homogeneous). Without this hack, foundational vowel rules like akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ wouldn't work mathematically.
3. The final phonetic cleanup
Once the grammatical engine has finished building the word (after 6.1.107 creates the final text string of Rāmam), the grammatical fiction is no longer needed.
Pāṇini uses his famous final sūtra, 8.4.68 (अ अ), as a global cleanup command. It translates to: "Let the short 'अ', which I treated as open (vivṛta) for grammatical computation, now return to its natural, closed (saṃvṛta) pronunciation for actual human speech."
Vidyut is acting as a strict state machine here. It sees the short 'अ' nestled inside the 'म', and mechanically triggers 8.4.68 at the very end of the Tripādī to lock in its final phonetic state.

notes.verdict: Claude 2026-11-16 — Accepted, and it corrects my earlier wording: 8.4.68 turns EVERY short a back to saṃvṛta (Kāśikā: 'akāro vivṛtaḥ saṃvṛto bhavati', vṛkṣaḥ, plakṣaḥ), not only a word-final a, and not long/pluta. So Vidyut is right to list it for rāmam. It changes no letter, so the form is unaffected. DECISION: S182 reworded to 'every short a'; implementing it needs an articulation field first, a coordinator job after the coverage run.
